value.overview: The Blue-chested Hummingbird (Polyerata amabilis) is a small, mainly lowland hummingbird of humid Central America and northwestern South America. It is named for the male’s brilliant blue-violet throat and upper breast, contrasting with bright green upperparts. The species often lives along forest edges, in second growth, clearings, gardens, and plantations rather than in the darkest forest interior. In Costa Rica it is a local resident, especially associated with humid Caribbean-slope habitats.
value.classification: The Blue-chested Hummingbird belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the emerald hummingbird group. It was formerly usually placed in the genus Amazilia but is now treated as Polyerata amabilis.
value.identification: This small hummingbird is about 9 centimeters long, with a slender, mostly black bill and a compact body. The male has bright green crown and upperparts, a strongly iridescent blue-violet throat and chest, and darker lower underparts. The female is duller, with bronze-green upperparts and a pale, spotted throat and breast that may show bluish feathers. In both sexes, the tail is relatively dark, and the bird’s rapid wingbeats and hovering flight are typical of hummingbirds.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southeastern Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama, continuing into western Colombia and western Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is a local resident rather than a widespread common hummingbird. It is most reliably associated with the humid Caribbean lowlands and foothills, including areas south of Limón and near Manzanillo, and may occur locally along forest edges and lower mountain passes. It uses moist lowland forest, open woodland, second growth, streamside vegetation, plantations, rural gardens, and flowering clearings, generally below about 500 meters but locally higher.
value.migrationStatus: Resident and non-migratory. In Costa Rica, individuals are expected year-round in suitable Caribbean-slope habitat, although local movements may follow flowering and food availability.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited compared with that of better-studied hummingbirds. Available accounts indicate that breeding may occur during the drier part of the year, approximately February through May in parts of the range. The female builds a small cup-shaped nest, often on a horizontal branch of a low tree or shrub near a forest edge, usually only a few meters above the ground. A clutch normally contains two small white eggs, and the female provides the incubation and care of the young.
value.dietFeeding: The Blue-chested Hummingbird feeds mainly on nectar from flowering trees, shrubs, vines, and herbs. It commonly forages along forest margins and in open areas where flowers are scattered. It may follow a regular trapline between nectar sources, but it can also defend particularly productive flowers or feeding patches. Small insects and other arthropods provide important protein, especially for females and growing nestlings, and are captured in short aerial sallies or gleaned from foliage.
value.behavior: It is active by day and usually forages alone, moving quickly between flowers with hovering flight. Individuals may perch quietly in shrubs or low branches between feeding bouts. Males can defend feeding territories, particularly when flowers are scarce, while courtship may involve display flights or temporary groupings of males. The species tolerates some disturbance and can visit gardens and plantations, but it remains local where suitable flowering vegetation and forest cover are limited.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains fairly common in suitable habitat in parts of its range.
